info.name: Java Interview Lab
info.description: Interactive labs for java-interview-lab. Each folder follows RESET -> BAD -> STATE -> GOOD -> STATE AFTER GOOD. See docs/INTERACTIVE_LABS.md.

request.description:
WHAT AM I LEARNING: Hibernate's persistence context tracks managed entities and flushes changes (dirty checking) automatically at transaction commit - you never call save()/update() for a field mutation on a managed entity; but a DETACHED entity's changes are silently lost.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: PersistenceLifecycleService's detached-mutation method (BAD) and renameViaDirtyCheckingOnly (GOOD, changeName() call).

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD - the mutation on a detached entity never reaches the database (no UPDATE SQL logged). GOOD - an UPDATE is logged automatically at commit, with no explicit save() call.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Watch the console for `Hibernate: update ...` lines - they appear only at transaction commit for the GOOD path, and never for the BAD path.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What is dirty checking, and why does calling a setter on a detached entity not persist the change?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: A @Transactional method rolls back ALL its database changes if it throws an unchecked exception - partial writes are never committed.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: TransactionLabController's bad()/good() delegate methods, at the point right before the exception is thrown.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD - after the exception, the earlier write in the SAME transaction is GONE (rolled back) when you query state afterward. GOOD - the write survives because it commits cleanly.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Call BAD, then STATE, and see that the record the method tried to write does not exist - the whole transaction rolled back, not just the failing statement.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: If an exception is thrown halfway through a @Transactional method, what happens to the database writes that already ran?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: REQUIRES_NEW starts a genuinely separate, independent transaction that commits/rolls back on its own - but only when invoked through the Spring proxy (a separate bean), never via self-invocation (this.).

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: the self-invocation BAD method and the separate-bean GOOD method, plus the underlying REQUIRES_NEW method itself.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD (self-invocation) - REQUIRES_NEW is silently ignored, everything runs in the SAME outer transaction. GOOD (separate bean) - the inner REQUIRES_NEW transaction really commits independently, even if the outer transaction later rolls back.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Trigger REQUIRES_NEW BAD, then STATE, then the GOOD variant, then STATE AFTER GOOD - compare whether the inner write survived an outer rollback in each case.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: Why doesn't REQUIRES_NEW create a real nested transaction when called via this from the same class?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: READ_COMMITTED allows a non-repeatable read (a value you read once can change if you read it again in the same transaction, because another transaction committed in between); REPEATABLE_READ prevents this by holding a consistent snapshot.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: IsolationAnomalyLab's two reads inside the same transaction, with a concurrent writer transaction running in between.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: READ_COMMITTED - the second read inside the same transaction returns a DIFFERENT value than the first (anomaly reproduced). REPEATABLE_READ - both reads return the SAME value (anomaly prevented).

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Compare the two JSON responses field by field - firstRead vs secondRead.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What is a non-repeatable read, and which isolation level is the minimum needed to prevent it?

item.name: 10 Dirty read - READ_UNCOMMITTED (Postgres upgrades it, never dirty)

request.description:
WHAT AM I LEARNING: Optimistic locking (a @Version column) detects a lost-update conflict at commit time by comparing version numbers - it does NOT block concurrent transactions, it lets them race and then rejects the loser with a real OptimisticLockException.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: OptimisticLockingLabController's bad()/good() methods, at the point where two REAL, separately-committed transactions both read the same row before either writes.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD - the second transaction's write silently overwrites the first (lost update, if concurrency control is bypassed). GOOD - the second transaction's commit throws a genuine OptimisticLockException because the @Version column no longer matches.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Check the DB via DBeaver after each scenario - the version column value and whether both writers' changes are reflected or only one.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: How does @Version-based optimistic locking detect a conflict, and what exception does it throw?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: Pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) makes a second transaction physically WAIT for the row-level lock to be released, rather than racing and failing later.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: PessimisticLockingLabController's good() method, right at the SELECT ... FOR UPDATE call, and the second concurrent request's equivalent call.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD - two concurrent readers/writers race with no lock, one can overwrite the other. GOOD - the second request BLOCKS until the first transaction commits or rolls back.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: In DBeaver, run `SELECT * FROM pg_locks WHERE relation = 'lab_account'::regclass;` while a pessimistic-lock request is in flight to see the real row lock held.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What is the difference between SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and optimistic locking, and when would you choose one over the other?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: A fixed thread pool's size and its queue capacity are two SEPARATE things - a small pool with an unbounded queue can silently accept unlimited work and grow memory forever; rejection policies (AbortPolicy/CallerRunsPolicy) change what happens when a BOUNDED queue is full.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: ExecutorLabController.bad() at the `tpe.getQueue().size()` line.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD - the queue size grows without bound as tasks are submitted faster than they complete. AbortPolicy - later submissions throw RejectedExecutionException. CallerRunsPolicy - the calling thread itself executes the rejected task instead of throwing.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Compare pool size (fixed) against queue size (growing) in the BAD response.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What happens when a ThreadPoolExecutor's queue is full, and what do the different RejectedExecutionHandler policies do differently?

item.name: 07 DiscardOldestPolicy (oldest queued task dropped, id=2 never runs)

request.description:
WHAT AM I LEARNING: supplyAsync() returns immediately without blocking - the actual work runs concurrently on a separate thread; chaining .thenApply()/.get() sequentially instead of composing with allOf() forces work back into serial execution, wasting the parallelism.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: ComposedAggregationService.aggregateConcurrently() at the CompletableFuture.allOf(...) line.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: SEQUENTIAL (bad) - total duration is roughly the SUM of each individual call's duration. PARALLEL (good) - total duration is roughly the MAX of the individual durations, because they ran concurrently.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Compare totalDuration between the two responses - it should be dramatically smaller for PARALLEL given the same simulated per-call delays.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: Why does calling .join() immediately after each supplyAsync() call defeat the purpose of using CompletableFuture at all?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: @Async, like @Transactional, only takes effect through the Spring proxy - calling an @Async method via this from inside the same bean runs it SYNCHRONOUSLY on the calling thread, not asynchronously.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: the self-invocation BAD method and the separate-bean GOOD method, checking Thread.currentThread().getName() at the point the supposedly-async work executes.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD - the async method runs on the SAME thread as the caller (proxy bypassed). GOOD - it runs on a DIFFERENT thread from Spring's task executor.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Compare the threadName field in each response - BAD and the caller's thread should match; GOOD should differ.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: Why doesn't @Async actually run asynchronously when called from another method in the same class?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: ThreadLocal state outlives the logical task that set it - in a reused thread pool worker, a value set by one task is still visible to the NEXT unrelated task on the same thread unless you explicitly call remove() in a finally block.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: ThreadLocalLabController.bad() at the second Future's submission, and the GOOD variant's try/finally remove() call.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD - task2 (unrelated to task1) sees task1's leftover correlation id on the reused worker thread. GOOD - each task sees a clean/correct ThreadLocal value because the previous task removed its own.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Compare the correlationId returned for task2 in BAD vs GOOD.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: Why is ThreadLocal.remove() mandatory when using ThreadLocal with a pooled ExecutorService?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: @Service beans are singletons by default (shared, so mutable state races); prototype beans give a fresh instance per lookup, but only when accessed via ObjectProvider or a scoped proxy, never via a plain injected field; request/session/application scopes are backed by REAL Spring web-scope proxies, not manually-created objects; bean creation follows a fixed order (constructor -> BeanPostProcessor.before -> @PostConstruct -> BeanPostProcessor.after).

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: MutableSingletonPriceService.calculateDiscountedPrice() (singleton race), SingletonWithObjectProvider.getWorkerId() (prototype), RequestScopedIdHolder/SessionScopedIdHolder constructors, BeanLifecycleDemoBean's constructor/@PostConstruct and BeanLifecycleLoggingPostProcessor.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: singleton race under concurrent load can produce a wrong price; prototype calls return a DIFFERENT worker id each time; request scope returns the SAME id twice within one HTTP call but a DIFFERENT id across two separate calls; session scope stays STABLE across calls sharing a cookie and changes once cookies are cleared.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: For session scope (GET /lab/scopes/session), Postman's Cookie Jar handles this automatically - the server sets a JSESSIONID cookie on the first response, Postman stores it and resends it on every later request from the SAME cookie jar/environment, so the sessionScopedId stays IDENTICAL across repeated calls. To see a NEW id: open Postman's Cookies manager (link under the Send button, or Settings > Cookies) and remove the JSESSIONID cookie for this host, or run the request from a different environment/cookie jar - the very next call gets a fresh session and a fresh id.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What's the actual difference between prototype scope and request scope, and why is a mutable field in a singleton dangerous?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: Spring AOP advice (e.g. @Around, @Transactional, @Async) is woven at PROXY boundaries, not into the target class bytecode. Calling a method via this from inside the same bean completely bypasses the proxy, so the advice never runs.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: SelfInvocationTimingService.processOrder() and .slowStep() (BAD path); OrderProcessingService.processOrder() and SlowStepService.slowStep() (GOOD path); ExecutionTimeAspect.trackExecutionTime() (should NOT hit in BAD, SHOULD hit in GOOD).

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: In BAD, aspectIntercepted will be false because this.slowStep() never crosses the proxy. In GOOD, aspectIntercepted will be true with a real measured executionTimeMs.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Call POST self-invocation/bad, then GET proxy-info to see the real runtime class names (CGLIB proxy suffix on SlowStepService, not on SelfInvocationTimingService via the this-call).

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: Why doesn't @Transactional/@Async work when called from another method in the same class?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: Swallowing an exception (empty catch block) silently hides a real failure; rethrowing only the message (`throw new RuntimeException(e.getMessage())`) loses the original stack trace and cause chain, making production debugging much harder than wrapping with the original exception as `cause`.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: the swallowed-exception BAD method's empty/near-empty catch block, the lossy-rethrow BAD method's `new RuntimeException(e.getMessage())` line, and the GOOD method's `new RuntimeException(msg, e)` line.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD (swallowed) - the caller never learns anything failed. BAD (lossy rethrow) - the resulting exception's getCause() is null, the original stack trace is gone. GOOD - getCause() returns the original exception, full stack trace preserved.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Inspect the HTTP error body for each scenario and compare whether a cause chain / original exception type is present.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: Why is `catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e.getMessage()); }` an anti-pattern, and what should you do instead?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: Lazy-loading a collection inside a loop over parent entities triggers ONE extra SELECT per parent (the N+1 problem) - fetch join / entity graph / DTO projection collapse this into a SINGLE query.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: the BAD method's loop over parents (watch Hibernate SQL logging in the console, count the SELECT statements), and the GOOD method's single fetch-join query.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD - console logs 1 SELECT for parents + N SELECTs (one per parent) for children. GOOD - console logs exactly 1 SELECT total, regardless of N.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Count the `Hibernate:` lines printed to the console for each scenario - the response also reports the measured query count directly.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What is the N+1 select problem, and what are the three main ways to fix it in JPA/Hibernate?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: these are early demo endpoints for optimistic/pessimistic locking retained for backward compatibility - prefer folders 05 and 06 (Optimistic Lock / Pessimistic Lock) for the fully-specified, audited version of these labs.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: see folder 05/06 INFO entries.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: same behavior as folders 05/06.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: same as folders 05/06.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: see folder 05/06 INFO entries.

WHAT AM I LEARNING: replacing an if/else chain that picks payment logic by type with the Strategy pattern (a PaymentStrategy interface + a Factory that resolves the right implementation by key) makes adding a new payment method a pure addition (new class + factory entry), not an edit to existing branching logic.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: the BAD if/else dispatcher and the GOOD factory's strategy-resolution line, plus the chosen PaymentStrategy implementation's pay() method.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD and GOOD produce the SAME business result for CREDIT_CARD, but GOOD resolves the WALLET/BANK_TRANSFER strategies without touching any conditional branching code.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Compare the responses for CREDIT_CARD (both BAD and GOOD) then WALLET and BANK_TRANSFER (GOOD only, no BAD equivalent needed to prove the point).

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: How does the Strategy pattern avoid the open/closed principle violation of a growing if/else or switch statement?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: Circuit Breaker trips from CLOSED to OPEN after a failure threshold, then rejects calls immediately (fail-fast) without even attempting them, then probes recovery via HALF_OPEN; Retry re-attempts a failing call a bounded number of times; RateLimiter caps calls per time window; Bulkhead caps concurrent calls; Timeout aborts a call that runs too long; Fallback supplies a default response when all else is exhausted.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: ResilienceLabController's individual scenario methods, and the underlying Resilience4j-annotated service methods (@CircuitBreaker/@Retry/@RateLimiter/@Bulkhead/@TimeLimiter/@Fallback).

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: Circuit Breaker - after enough failures, the circuit state visibly changes to OPEN and subsequent calls are rejected WITHOUT executing the underlying method at all. Retry - a call that fails twice then succeeds on the third attempt returns success, with the retry count visible in the response.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Call the RESET endpoint between scenarios so state doesn't bleed across experiments; watch the response's reported state/attempt counters.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What are the states of a circuit breaker, and what triggers each transition?

EXTERNAL DEPENDENCY CONFIG: POST /api/labs/resilience/external/config with a body like {"failNext": 10, "delayMs": 0} (or {"alwaysFail": true}) arms the fake FlakyExternalService BEFORE you trigger a scenario - GET /api/labs/resilience/external/state lets you verify what's currently armed. The circuit-breaker scenario specifically relies on this: it no longer configures failures itself, so calling it without a prior /external/config leaves the circuit CLOSED the whole time (every call just succeeds) - that itself is a real, observable lesson about configuration-dependent behavior.

WHAT AM I LEARNING: Spring Security's filter chain intercepts every request before it reaches a controller; a JWT-based endpoint returns 401 with no token, 403 when the token is valid but lacks the required authority/role, and 200 only when both authentication AND authorization succeed.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: the JWT filter's token-validation method, and SecurityLabController's protected/admin-only endpoints.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: no token -> 401. valid USER token on an ADMIN-only endpoint -> 403. valid ADMIN token on the same endpoint -> 200.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Log in as USER and ADMIN separately, save each JWT into the jwt_token environment variable, then compare the three response status codes directly.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What's the practical difference between a 401 and a 403 response, and where in the Spring Security filter chain does each originate?

item.name: 01 LOGIN as USER (copy token into jwt_token env var)
05 LOGIN as ADMIN (copy token into jwt_token env var)

request.description:
WHAT AM I LEARNING: count++ is NOT atomic - it is read, increment, write as three separate steps (getfield/iadd/putfield). When multiple threads interleave these steps, updates are lost. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() uses a hardware CAS instruction to make the same operation a single, indivisible step.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: UnsynchronizedIntCounter.increment() (count++ line) for BAD; AtomicCounterService.increment() for GOOD. Open the Threads panel while stopped to see many worker threads stopped at the exact same line.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD - actual will be LESS than expected (200000), and the exact lost count will differ every run (nondeterministic). GOOD - actual will EXACTLY equal expected, every single run.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Run BAD several times with the same threads/increments and see lostUpdates change each time - this is the entire point: race conditions are not a fixed, reproducible number.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: Why is count++ not thread-safe, and how does AtomicInteger fix it without using a lock?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: synchronized and ReentrantLock both provide MUTUAL EXCLUSION - only one thread may be in the critical section at a time - but ReentrantLock gives you an explicit lifecycle (lock()/unlock()) you can observe as a log. ReadWriteLock lets MULTIPLE readers proceed concurrently while excluding writers. StampedLock's optimistic read takes NO lock at all and validates afterward.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: LockingPrimitivesLabController.runLockLifecycleDemo() at lifecycleLog.add(...LOCK_ACQUIRED) and maxConcurrentHolders.updateAndGet(...); IntrinsicMonitorCounter.incrementViaMethod(); ReadWriteLockCache.withReadLockHeld(...); StampedLockPoint.distanceFromOrigin() at tryOptimisticRead()/validate().

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: reentrant-lock/bad -> maxConcurrentHolders will be measured GREATER THAN 1 (no mutual exclusion). reentrant-lock/good -> maxConcurrentHolders will be measured EXACTLY 1, every run. read-write-lock/demo -> all readers acquire concurrently (fast). stamped-lock/demo -> distanceFromOrigin = 5.0 with no lock ever taken.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Compare the lifecycleLog array between bad and good - in bad, multiple workers' ATTEMPTING_LOCK/LOCK_ACQUIRED entries interleave BEFORE any WORK entry; in good, each worker's four log lines appear as a clean, uninterrupted block.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What is the actual difference between synchronized and ReentrantLock? When would you reach for ReadWriteLock or StampedLock instead?

item.name: 03 ReentrantLock BAD (no lock, lifecycle log, 4 threads)
08 ABA problem BAD (AtomicReference CAS false positive)

request.description:
WHAT AM I LEARNING: volatile guarantees VISIBILITY (a write is immediately visible to other threads) but NOT atomicity. A compound operation like count++ (read-modify-write) STILL races even on a volatile field. volatile is correct ONLY for single reads/writes (like a stop flag), never for compound updates.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: VolatileCounter.increment() (count++ line) for the misconception check; ShutdownFlagWorker.requestStop() (single assignment) for the correct-usage case.

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: misconception-check -> stillRaced will be true, actual less than expected, EVEN THOUGH the field is volatile. correct-usage -> workerStoppedWithinTimeout will be true - a single volatile assignment IS enough here because there's no compound operation involved.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: Run misconception-check several times - the lost-update pattern looks IDENTICAL to the plain (non-volatile) race-condition lab, proving volatile alone did not fix it.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: If I mark a counter volatile, is it now thread-safe? Why or why not?

WHAT AM I LEARNING: five backend-realistic pattern applications in the SAME checkout/payment domain (not toy Dog/Cat/Shape examples) - Factory (PaymentStrategyFactory resolves ANY PaymentStrategy bean, Strategy AND Adapter implementations alike), Adapter (ExternalPaymentProviderAdapter hides a genuinely incompatible third-party SDK contract - cents as long, integer status codes - behind the app's own PaymentStrategy interface), Observer (OrderPlacementService publishes a real Spring ApplicationEvent that TWO independent @EventListener beans react to, with zero coupling to the publisher), Builder (OrderRequest is immutable and only exists fully-validated, after build() succeeds), Proxy (GreeterProxyFactory is a minimal, from-scratch JDK dynamic proxy - the same mechanism Spring's own @Transactional/@Async/@Aspect proxies are built on; compare with the REAL Spring CGLIB proxy at GET /api/labs/aop/proxy-info).

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: ExternalPaymentProviderAdapter.pay() (Adapter); OrderPlacementService.placeOrder() + InventoryReservationListener/EmailNotificationListener.onOrderPlaced() (Observer); OrderRequest.Builder.build() (Builder, the validation-throw line); GreeterProxyFactory.withLogging()'s InvocationHandler lambda (Proxy).

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: adapter/bad duplicates the cent-conversion logic at the call site; adapter/good hides it entirely behind PaymentStrategy. observer/place-order flips BOTH listeners' state from a single publishEvent() call. builder/build-invalid throws IllegalStateException from inside build() itself, never producing a half-built object. proxy/with-logging shows before:greet/after:greet bracketing the real call; proxy/without-logging shows neither.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: compare adapter/bad vs adapter/good's response shape (raw status code vs clean PaymentStrategy result); compare proxy/without-logging vs proxy/with-logging's interceptionLog array.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: Give a REAL example (not Dog/Cat) of Factory, Adapter, Observer, Builder and Proxy you've actually used, and explain what problem each one solved.

item.name: 02 Adapter BAD (raw SDK call, cent conversion duplicated)
09 Proxy - with logging (JDK dynamic proxy interception)

request.description:
WHAT AM I LEARNING: a lazy JPA relationship is a proxy that can only be initialized while its Hibernate session is open - accessing it AFTER the owning @Transactional method returns throws a REAL LazyInitializationException. Separately, a FetchType.EAGER relationship is loaded on EVERY load of its owning entity, even when the calling code never reads it - trading N+1 for unconditional, unnecessary work.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: LazyInitializationDemoService.loadOrderWithoutTouchingItems() (watch the transaction/session end as the method returns); LazyEagerLabController.lazyBad() at order.getOrderItems().size() (the line that throws); LazyAccessWithinTransactionService.loadOrderAndCountItemsWithinTransaction() (access happens INSIDE the transaction); EagerFetchAlwaysLoadsService.sumQuantitiesOnly() (never touches product, yet triggers its query).

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: lazy/bad throws a genuine LazyInitializationException with threwLazyInitializationException=true. lazy/good returns the same count successfully because access happens before the transaction ends. eager/bad reports queriesTouchingProductTable > 0 even though the method's own code never reads OrderItem.getProduct().

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: compare the two lazy responses' threwLazyInitializationException field; for eager, compare totalQueries and queriesTouchingProductTable to see the hidden cost.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: Why does accessing a lazy collection outside its transaction throw LazyInitializationException, and why is making every relationship EAGER not a real fix for N+1?

item.name: 02 Lazy BAD (access outside transaction, real LazyInitializationException)
04 Eager BAD (product joined even though never read)

request.description:
WHAT AM I LEARNING: Cache-Aside (lazy loading) means the APPLICATION manages the cache explicitly - read checks the cache first and only falls through to the database on a miss (populating the cache afterward); write goes to the database first, then INVALIDATES (removes) the cache entry rather than trying to update it in place.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: NoCacheProductService.read() (BAD, every call increments databaseReadCount); CacheAsideProductService.read() at cache.get(id) (GOOD, the miss/hit branch); CacheAsideProductService.write() at cache.remove(id) (invalidate-not-update).

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: calling bad/read three times in a row increments databaseReadCount to 3. Calling good/read three times in a row increments databaseReadCount to 1 only (first call is a miss, the next two are hits). After good/write, the next good/read is a miss again (cache was invalidated, not updated).

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: compare databaseReadCount growth between the BAD and GOOD sequences for the SAME number of calls; watch isCachedNow flip to false immediately after a write.

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What is the Cache-Aside pattern, and why does a write typically invalidate the cache entry instead of updating it directly?

item.name: 02 BAD read (no cache, every call hits DB) x1
03 GOOD read (cache-aside, first call = miss) x1
04 GOOD read again (should now be a cache HIT)
05 GOOD write (DB write then cache INVALIDATE)
06 GOOD read after write (miss again - cache was invalidated)

request.description:
WHAT AM I LEARNING: a real, database-level deadlock - two concurrent transactions each hold a row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) the other one needs, in opposite orders (T1: A then B, T2: B then A). This is NOT a JVM-internal deadlock (no ThreadMXBean involved) - PostgreSQL's OWN deadlock detector notices the cycle and kills exactly one transaction with a real 'deadlock detected' error. Crucially, the HTTP request never hangs forever: Postgres's deadlock_timeout (default 1s) resolves the cycle almost immediately, and the controller also bounds every Future.get() with a timeout as a second safety net.

WHERE TO PUT BREAKPOINTS: InconsistentLockOrderTransferService.transferStock() at both findByIdForUpdate() calls (BAD); DeterministicOrderTransferService.transferStock() at the firstId/secondId ordering logic (GOOD).

WHAT I SHOULD PREDICT: BAD - exactly one of T1/T2 fails with a message containing 'deadlock detected', the other commits; total wall-clock time is close to Postgres's deadlock_timeout (about 1 second), not the 10-second bound. GOOD - both transactions commit, no deadlock, because both always lock the lower id first.

WHAT I SHOULD OBSERVE: run BAD several times - which of T1/T2 fails is NOT always the same (nondeterministic, depends on exact timing); stockConserved should always be true either way (100+100=200 total stock never lost).

WHAT INTERVIEW QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: What causes a database-level deadlock, how does Postgres resolve it, and what's the standard fix (consistent lock ordering)?

item.name: 02 BAD (inconsistent lock order - real Postgres deadlock)
